overall_summary: Deduplication of 47 unique shorts reveals a massive performance split: first-person/second-person immersive cosmic survival scenarios ('What If You Fell Into...') consistently deliver 400 to 1,030 views and industry-beating like-to-view ratios (~3.5%), whereas abstract psychology and repeated static trivia (brain memory illusions, songs stuck in head, recycled octopus/shark facts) crater below 100 views. Retention and engagement peak when extreme planetary conditions are framed as immediate, sensory human survival dilemmas.

winning_patterns.pattern: Second-Person Extreme Environment Survival ('What If You Fell Into...')
winning_patterns.evidence: 'What If You Fell Into a Liquid Diamond Planet?' (1,029 views, 38 likes) and 'What If You Fell Into the Planet of Burning Ice?' (972 views, 18 likes) dramatically outperformed channel averages.
winning_patterns.action: Anchor future videos in high-stakes hypothetical survival scenarios where the viewer is dropped into an alien or extreme biome.

winning_patterns.pattern: Bizarre Planetary Physics with Sensory Paradoxes
winning_patterns.evidence: 'The Planet Darker Than Coal: TrES-2b' (1,030 views, 36 likes) and 'This Planet Rains Supersonic Rubies!' (725 views, 25 likes) maintained top-tier views per day.
winning_patterns.action: Highlight tactile, visual paradoxes (metallic atmospheres, extreme vapor pressures, lethal temperatures) rather than dry astronomical distances.

weak_patterns.evidence: 'Your Brain Can Create Fake Memories' was posted multiple times generating only 5 to 53 views; 'The Real Reason Songs Get Stuck In Your Head' achieved just 17 views.
weak_patterns.action: Retire passive psychological trivia and ungrounded memory concepts; eliminate redundant re-uploads of identical facts.

weak_patterns.evidence: 'This Star Is Older Than the Universe!' (11 views) and 'The Eyeball Planet That Could Harbor Life!' (40 views) failed to spark curiosity.
weak_patterns.action: Avoid academic astronomical statements unless framed through a catastrophic or survival-driven lens.

next_video.concept: What If You Fell Into KELT-9b, The Star-Planet That Literally Tears Molecules Apart?
next_video.opening_direction: Open with an ultra-close-up of an astronaut visor reflecting a blinding blue-white inferno, accompanied by the urgent line: 'If you dropped into KELT-9b, you wouldn't just burn—your molecules would literally be torn to pieces.'
next_video.twist_direction: Reveal that the dayside temperature is hotter than 80% of all known stars (7,800°F), so hot that water and hydrogen cannot physically exist as molecules, creating an atmosphere of raw, vaporized iron and titanium tears.
next_video.reason: Capitalizes on the proven high-yield 'What If You Fell Into...' structure while introducing a completely unmentioned celestial monster (KELT-9b), avoiding saturated topics like diamond or burning ice planets.
fresh_topic_constraints: Must not reference TrES-2b, Gliese 436b, 55 Cancri e, WASP-76b, or Kepler-13Ab
Must not repeat diamond rain, ruby rain, glass rain, or molten iron rain
Must maintain under 22 seconds duration to maximize 100%+ completion loops

experiment: Test whether framing the twist around atomic disintegration ('molecules physically ripped apart') generates higher comments-per-view than standard heat/crush survival twists.
